subsubtopic: OBLIGATION TO CONSULT WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
It is time to puncture another Tory myth, Mr. Speaker. We all know the one about how Canada had to test the Cruise missile to prove we are loyal to NATO. That myth was laid to rest when Australia withdrew its support for MX missile testing. The American Secretary of State then pointed out that missile testing had nothing to do with its military alliance. Now we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) saying that Canada should support the American Strategic Defence Initiative. He says star wars is only prudent research to keep up with the Soviet Union. That's nonsense.
The U.S. Undersecretary of Defence Policy now admits that star wars is "the very core of our long-term policy. It's central," he says. In the face of this revelation, the Secretary of State for External Affairs doesn't lose his head. He keeps it firmly planted in the sand. Meanwhile, Canada is getting sucked deeper and deeper into defensive weapons. This new strategy is reshaping our northern defences. The Minister says we are only talking about a warning system.
Military experts say star wars weapons would have to be based in Canada. The Minister says: "We'll wait and see". Canada's Chief of Defence Research says star wars would be controlled by NORAD. The Minister says: "We'll wait and see". What are we waiting for? The Minister has the right and the obligation to consult with the Americans about future activities of NORAD. That duty is explicit in the 1981 NORAD renewal agreement. The Minister is ignoring that responsibility to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, in recent weeks there has been considerable criticism of the detention centres for applicants for refugee status. These centres are used for people who claimed refugee status but have been denied such status by officers of the Department of Employment and Immigration at one of Canada's points of entry. Pending a final decision on their case, these people are sent to detention centres.
In Toronto, refugee status applicants were not informed about the existence of volunteer, church and humanitarian organizations that would be prepared to provide legal aid. Sometimes they are given the Yellow Pages. A number of applicants were questioned by RCMP officers without being given access to a lawyer. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms is being violated, but officials of the Department of Employment and Immigration have stated that the Charter does not apply since the claimants are not Canadian citizens. There is a double standard being used here, one for Canadians and one for non-Canadians. We must not forget that this, too, is racism.

subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-TRIBUTE TO WORK OF PARTICIPANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of attending the First Ministers' Conference on the Economy in my home province of Saskatchewan as an official observer. Today I wish to share with the House some of my observations.
It was the beginning of a new era of First Ministers' conferences. The conference sessions were conducted in a positive atmosphere of co-operation, a refreshing change from the past. Moreover, this harmonious atmosphere extended beyond the reach of the cameras and microphones; it also characterized the working relations between the federal and provincial officials.
At a time of scarce financial resources it was apparent that all First Ministers were prepared to rise to the challenge of sharing their expertise and experiences, in trying to avoid the wasteful duplication of the past. Co-operation and consultation are fundamental to this Government's mandate and were clearly apparent in the conference initiatives and discussions. Employment, trade, investment, and interest rates were discussed objectively and without bitterness. For the first time we saw 11 First Ministers of all political persuasions working toward a goal of economic recovery.
We cannot expect that all the intergovernmental differences will be solved in one two-day session. We can and should expect continued joint efforts by all First Ministers in resolving differences in order to achieve the best solutions for all Canadians. That takes genuine trust and mutual respect, and I observed both among all the participants in Regina. I heartily applaud the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for initiating a new era-

February 25, 1985
Mr. Speaker, last week I attended a meeting with the President of Canada Post, my colleague from Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), Shirley Carr of the Canadian Labour Congress and councillor Marlene Carterill of the City of Ottawa. subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CN DOUBLE TRACKING PLANS ON BRITISH COLUMBIA RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of 36 Indian bands whose reserves will be seriously affected by CN's twin tracking program in central British Columbia, I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), along with the Transport Committee Chairman and the Chairman of the Fisheries and Forestry Committee to do whatever is necessary to stop CN from proceeding with its present double tracking plans along the sensitive Fraser-Thompson River corridor.
Since the Committee plans to hold hearings into the twin tracking program in mid-March, the Minister should postpone approval of the project at Mile 59-69 of the Ashcroft sub-division, considering that CN plans to begin dumping ballast into the Thompson River on or about March 1. The Native Alliance on CN Double Tracking believes that a one-year delay is needed to assess many unresolved environmental, social, and economic issues relating to the program properly, as well as time to determine whether the project is required by the western Canadian transport system, and to determine why the two railways cannot co-operate in this area and obtain a twin tracking option as a result.
While approval of the project is likely in the best interests of the CN corporation, it is certainly not in the best interest of the native people who live along the tracks in this area, and of the West Coast salmon fishery. The Government surely has a responsibility to put the needs of native people and a major fishery before a Crown corporation. Postponing this project would demonstrate its correct priority.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR GOVERNMENT'S REFUSAL OF $100 MILLION GRANT TO DOMTAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, my question is directed to the Parliamentary Secretary.
Taking advantage of the fact that Parliament was not in session, the Minister announced last week that the Government has decided to turn down a $100 million grant for Domtar. Since this Government has emphasized many times the importance of proper forest management and of our exports, what are the reasons behind this decision which may cause Quebec's economy to lose as many as 4,000 jobs?

subsubtopic: REASON FOR GOVERNMENT'S REFUSAL OF $100 MILLION GRANT TO DOMTAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister, who is out of the country on government business, I might tell the Hon. Member that the company which has made the application is essentially sound, as is the application itself. The Government, however, in its wisdom, has thought it important to decline money at this time on the grounds that to fund the application would be disruptive of the market. There are five other major companies waiting in line with similar submissions. To give the money that is requested to Domtar would be to place the Government in an almost impossible position to decline the requests of the other companies. I might say that the company in question has already received some $20 million from the Government under different auspices, and at different times. The final consideration, which the Hon. Member might also want to take into account, is the possibility that the Government of the United States would consider any subvention from us for this purpose a contravention of GATT type agreements.

Mr. Speaker, could the Minister inform the House whether the Government consulted with the Government of Quebec which has already paid out $85 million, and does the Government realize that without its contribution, this project may have to be cancelled?

Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, the Government did deliberate very carefully on the application. The Government viewed the plans of the company in question as sound, and recognized the contribution that would be made to the relevant province and to the economy as a whole should the project go ahead. However, after a lot of consideration, it thought it not desirable to approve the application and the funds in connection with it. Instead, it recommended very strongly that the company might wish to seek other sources of funds available in the private sector.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMPANY'S INVESTMENT IN UNITED STATES
CANADIAN COMPANY'S INVESTMENT IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the same Minister. In his response the Minister mentioned the Government of the United States and the possible reaction by that body to an investment by the Canadian Government in the Domtar Mill. Last December, Great Lakes Forest Products of Thunder Bay announced that it was building a major pulp and paper mill in Washington State to compete directly with paper mills in British Columbia. Can the Minister advise this House how, on one hand, the Government is prepared to allow a Canadian company, which has received a lot of money from the taxpayers, to invest in the United States to take away our jobs, and is not prepared to support a company in Canada to build in Canada to protect existing jobs?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMPANY'S INVESTMENT IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the premise of the question is wrong, as is the conclusion. This Government has been more generous in funding legitimate applications in a short period of time, something like 25 weeks in office, than the previous Government was in any comparable period. We have considered each application on its own merits. In the case of Domtar we found it inadvisable that the Government of Canada should spend the kind of funds that were requested, given the market conditions that prevailed both in Canada and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, on one hand a number of pulp and paper companies in Canada have received those kinds of grants in the past. There is no question that help was not needed because of the way the Liberals wanted to deal with things. Will the Minister advise the House whether he will now reconsider the Domtar application and look at the Great Lakes Forest Products investment in the United States and tell that company to bring its money back to Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member will appreciate that circumstances in the marketplace change. At a time when the Government of Canada, including the previous administration, looked kindly on certain applications, market conditions were very different from those that prevail now. The Domtar application was viewed in light of circumstances now, not in light of circumstances that prevailed two or three years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. The 27 cars of a freight train derailed at Petawawa yesterday morning has once again focused the serious attention of
February 25, 1985

Canadians on the transportation of dangerous goods. While local police, the fire department, and ambulance services were on the job and efficient, I ask the Minister how many more accidents will have to take place before he vigorously applies the regulations of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act passed in the last Parliament?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to receive the representations of the Hon. Member. He will know that the regulations for the transportation of dangerous goods have just been promulgated and they will take effect in stages over a period of time. There has been some resistance within the transportation sector, but I am pleased that the Hon. Member, and I assume he is speaking on behalf of his Party, will support that.
With respect to the specific accident in question, 1 am pleased to advise the House that the CTC is investigating the situation and I expect a report will be handed down in due course.
Mr. Speaker, why has the Minister allowed a shoddy standard of maintenance on the railways such that a broken rail caused 27 cars, three of which burned, to go off the rails on the CP main line?
Since September, why have you allowed this?

Will the Minister give a personal undertaking to see to it that all the rails are thoroughly inspected at all times and special emphasis is placed on the inspection of bridges during flood conditions such as these?
Up until September it was maintained thoroughly.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Members would agree that it would be rather presumptuous for me to accept the findings of the Hon. Member unless he has been monitoring the track during this period of time. If he has been, he should have reported such to the CTC.
I will certainly await the report of the CTC. I think they are perfectly qualified to conduct the investigation, and, whatever corrective action is required, this Minister will take such action.

FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has Finally put this matter before the House for debate. I believe the agriculture paper which was tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) three or four weeks ago is a very important document. I assume that the motion which the Government House Leader read to the House is the same motion as that which was in the preliminary draft which he gave to our House Leader a few days before the recess. At that time our House Leader indicated that we wanted a short debate with one or two speakers from our Party. Therefore, I appreciate that I have been provided with that opportunity this afternoon. However, in the future I wish that a motion such as this would be put on the Order Paper as that is the proper parliamentary procedure. If that is done, unanimous consent will not have to be sought as it was this afternoon, although that procedure works fine as long as everyone agrees.
The paper which was tabled by the Minister of Finance has raised a great deal of concern in the agricultural community. If we look at the press reports about the paper we would realize the reason for the concern. The press report of The Gazette on January 14 outlined the commitment which the Conservative Party made during the election campaign, which was to "establish an agri-bond program to provide loans at reduced interest rates to agricultural producers".
The article continued:
A tax exemption for earned income on these bonds will be provided to attract investment capital to this program.
The Conservative Party during the election campaign also indicated:
-tax rules for part-time farmers would be changed "to reflect the principles of equity, neutrality, simplicity and certainty" and arbitrary actions by the Revenue Department will be abolished.
The discussion paper which is now before the House makes no reference to the campaign commitments. It makes one

February 25, 1985
Tax Issues in Agriculture
wonder whether the campaign commitments have been totally forgotten by the Government. It is disturbing that the paper went on to point out that farmers pay some 4 per cent of their total farm income in income taxes. The paper goes on to suggest:
The proposed changes in the taxation of capital gains and the agri-bond concept raise questions about unfair competition, the potential for upward pressure on farm land prices and fairness vis-a-vis other taxpayers.
It continues:
Changing the $5,000 limit on farm losses a part-time farmer now can claim could jeopardize the position of full-time farmers-
That press report was of some concern to farmers across the country, but the press report of The Globe and Mail on February 23 gave them greater concern. The headline of the The Globe and Mail article read: "Study shows farmers earn twice as much as average Canadian". The Globe and Mail article outlined the white paper, which suggests that farmers are well off, that they have special tax concessions and that they do not pay their fair share of taxes.
I believe the allegations which were made in the newspaper reports and in the white paper are completely false and will not stand up to a close examination of the facts which exist in the agricultural community today. I would be surprised if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), who unfortunately is not with us this afternoon, would want to adopt this paper as it now stands. If he does, it will be apparent that he has lost the battle in Cabinet on this paper to the Minister of Finance and the Department of Finance. The paper obviously reflects the view of the Department of Finance more than the view of the Minister of Agriculture and certainly of the agricultural community across the country. We could compare it with the battle which was waged at Meech Lake over the consultation paper that the Government drafted on social policy. In that case the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) clearly won the day and the Minister of Finance lost. If we looked at this paper we would see that the Minister of Finance and his Department controlled the battle which took place over the drafting and writing of the white paper on farm taxation issues. The paper does not reflect the true financial difficulties which farmers face today.
If we looked at the income situation for farmers over the last 10 years, from 1974 to 1984, we would see that net farm incomes in 1974 were almost $3.6 billion. Ten years later, in 1984, the net realized farm income is $5.8 billion. For a document which has the Minister of Finance's name on it, and which is supposedly supported by the Minister of Agriculture and the Tory caucus, to suggest that farmers earn twice as much as other taxpayers and have an exceptionally good position in the income scale of the country does not square with the facts which are evident in the agricultural community. We have only to look back at the Farm Credit Corporation report of last fall. It indicated that 39,000 farmers were in serious financial difficulty. That does not mean that those farmers are having trouble buying a new car. We are talking about people with equity which is less than 15 per cent. That is the criterion of the study. They are paying over 40 per cent of
their gross income to meet their debt payments. They were borrowing more than they were investing in capital expenditures.
This paper does not really reflect the tough financial situation about which many farmers complain. As a matter of fact, when one looks through the paper one sees that the calculation of income is based on capital gain. How can a farmer take a capital gain which might exist on his property and go out and buy seed, fuel or fertilizer? That is just ridiculous. If there were a sharp capital gain during the mid-1970s, there certainly has been a dramatic, precipitous and disastrous capital loss in the last two or three years, and that is reflected in the Farm Credit Corporation report which was published in November of this year.
Therefore, I would point out to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture that this report really does not accurately reflect the income or the tax position of many farmers. For instance, it is pointed out that the income of full-time farmers in 1982 was $16,000 and the income of all non-farm tax filers was $16,732. On the previous page it points out that the average farmer in Canada has an equity investment of $416,000. When there is an equity capital investment of that amount and the farmer works 16 hours a day along with his wife and family, and he ends up with a net income of $16,000, he really is not even getting a decent return on his investment. He gets nothing for his labour, his wife's labour, and in many cases the labour of family members. So I feel that this report of the Minister of Finance is most unfair and does not accurately represent the financial situation of the farm community.
I talked to several farm families over the weekend who are really appalled at the way the Government has presented the position of farm families in this country. The report indicates the return on investment, including debt, in the years 1977 to 1983 varied between 2.4 per cent and 0 per cent. This provides practically nothing for wages and very little for the investment which the average farm producer has made.
I feel that we will need to have a very good discussion in the standing committee. We will want to know what kind of a tax expenditure the Minister of Finance is willing to commit to Canadian agriculture under an agri-bond system. We will want to know whether the Government really wants to keep its campaign commitment to abolish capital gains on farm land which continues to be used for agricultural purposes. But this document, at first blush, appears to be trying to do one of two things, or perhaps both; either it is a way to start the ball rolling for the Government to welsh on the three commitments it made during the election campaign, or else it is trying to present a rosy picture of the agricultural scene today in order to try to cover up the Government's lack of action on the farm debt crisis.
Clearly, one cannot read the Farm Credit Corporation report on the financial debt crisis of this country without coming to the conclusion that it is a very serious problem.
February 25, 1985

Farm properties have dropped anywhere from 25 per cent to 50 per cent in value. In many areas like northern Ontario or Timiskaming there has been a serious drop in farm value. This is not something which has just happened in this country. The United States is facing the same kind of problems. The only difference is that the United States has taken action and put in place various programs for their farmers where 25 per cent of a farmer's debt is set aside for a period of up to five years. Farm interest rates have been written down to 7 per cent or 5 per cent, and providing that puts the young farmer into a positive cash flow position, these benefits will be extended. But the United States has even gone beyond that in providing a loan guarantee system for finances which will assist its farmers.
I believe this paper is really designed to do one of two things; either to start in train a process so that the Government will be able to welsh on its campaign commitments relating to these three items, or to cover up as a smoke and mirrors show its lack of action for the serious financial debt crisis which is facing much of Canadian agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on a motion to refer the report on tax issues in agriculture, published by the Government in January 1985, to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, having listened to and read the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) in this House more than a week ago, on February 15, I feel some trepidation with respect to the Minister's attitude. The Minister, in this very House, accused Opposition Members of not wanting to refer this paper to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and I quote from Hansard at page 2402, Mr. Speaker:
It dumbfounds me to witness this continuing reluctance on behalf of the Official Opposition to give us an opportunity to refer these three items to an appropriate standing committee.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, and we know the Chair does not take sides in the House, the Minister misled us, probably involuntarily, but just the same, we must admit the Minister was not being entirely frank, not quite honest when he told the House that it was the Opposition's fault if this Government was refusing to go ahead and help farmers, because the exact opposite is true.
Mr. Speaker, the discussion paper was not published until January 1985. I think this is rather strange, considering the fact that last summer, in July and August, the Government seemed to be willing to help farmers at any level.

I would just like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, of some of the campaign promises which the Tories made last summer. No
Tax Issues in Agriculture
doubt like us Liberal Members, Mr. Speaker, you have had to listen to that litany of campaign promises which bored you as much as it bored us, I am afraid. However, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that there were specific promises made at that time to abolish the capital gains tax on the sale of farm property. There was no question then of issuing a document which would attempt to do the opposite or which would at least suggest that abolishing the capital gains tax would be difficult if not impossible.
The Tories also promised to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer agri-bonds. I have read this document, Mr. Speaker, and I can tell you that I am not convinced that the Government wants an issue of agri-bonds at all. I wonder why the Conservative Government during the election campaign could not have prepared a document which looked at the possibility of offering a program before they promised it to the public. It should have done that instead of offering the program and then going back to the electors of this country some four or five months later and accusing the Opposition of dragging its feet. It is the Conservatives who took four months to issue a document which they apparently were ready for in the month of August of last year, and in that same document they attempt to welsh on their promises.
This Government cannot have it that way, Mr. Speaker. Either it makes promises and intends to live with them, or just maybe those Hon. Members should stand up in this House and apologize to the Canadian public and tell the people of Canada: "We are sorry; we made 338 promises but we can only live with about four or five of them. Perhaps we didn't think about them properly". Maybe they should admit the mistakes they made last summer. They should not stand in the House intent on accusing the Opposition of dragging its feet and take five or six months to issue a consultation document when they claimed they were ready to implement a document of consultation last summer as well as to proceed with the legislation. This leads me to believe that when the Conservative Party was in opposition it thought that governing this country was a far easier job than it now finds it to be. That is probably because the Government did not think through its promises before making them.
The people of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell do not agree with the government reports we have been seeing in the last few weeks that farmers are in as good as or better a financial situation than others in the country. Our experience in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell has been quite the opposite. We have read in documents that the income of the average farmer is somewhat higher than that of people in business. The documents indicate that this is so as regards a full-time farmer versus people in business. They do not even specify whether the people in business are full-time or part-time. It could very well be that the people in full-time business of any kind make more than those who are not full-time. That still does not mean that the agricultural sector does not have a problem. The agricul-

February 25, 1985
Tax Issues in Agriculture
tural sector of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell has very serious problems.

Let me name just a few. Hog producers, in the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell have suffered serious losses in recent years. In one community in my riding, twelve hog producers went out of business because of bankruptcy. Their production represented 8,000 slaughter hogs per year. Six more producers went out of business voluntarily, as opposed to going bankrupt, representing a total production of 2,000 slaughter hogs per year. Add to this several fires during the last four or five years as a result of which we lost five more producers who had an annual production of 2,400 slaughter hogs.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear that the position of farmers in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is not that good. On behalf of my constituents, I want to say that we are waiting for the Progressive Conservative Party to come through with the promises it made during the last election campaign.

During the last election campaign the present Government, which was then the Opposition, proposed that it was going to extend and expand the Farm Credit Corporation special interest rate subsidy, that it would revise Section 31 of the Income Tax Act and do a variety of things for the farmers of the country. The people of my riding may not have voted Tory, but the day after the election they still expected the Government which had been elected to live up to the campaign promises it had made. But the Government did little or nothing. It only cut back. It made a series of cuts in agricultural programs. It has increased charges to the farmers of the country. The farmers of the country have been treated with very little respect.
One example of this lack of respect is that the Government has appointed a committee. In his speech to the Canadian Club of Toronto on February 13, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) announced the names of certain individuals who would be part of a study team on the agricultural program review. It is very important to outline this because it describes the attitude of the Government toward agriculture. I could not believe my eyes when I saw the list of the nine people appointed to this study team. None of them were farmers. None of the members were from western Canada. None of them were from the Maritimes. There were no women members and only one francophone. That is the type of committee the Government was in the process of establishing to review agricultural programs in the country. If those are the kind of people who are preparing Government programs, it is small wonder that they think everything is all right and that nothing needs to be improved. However, that is not the attitude of the farmers of the country. They require assistance from the Government.
It is our hope that sending this document to committee will persuade the Government to listen to the people of Canada. We hope the Government will listen to the farmers when they
send delegations to appear before the committee to tell the Government that its campaign promises should be respected. The farmers of the country need assistance. They need agribonds. If the Government did not intend to deliver on its promise of agri-bonds maybe it should not have made that promise.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to agree with this motion to strike a committee in the Department of Finance to study the question of capital gains tax, agri-bonds, and Section 31 of the Income Tax Act as they affect farmers. We are somewhat curious as to why it has taken three or four months from the time the Minister announced such a decision and what the reason for the delay was. Apparently the Minister would like an answer very quickly in order that some of the recommendations can be incorporated into his Budget. I am not sure that that will be possible.
If that is the Government's intention, I think it is regrettable that the basis of the discussion in the finance committee will be this white paper prepared by the Department of Finance. I say it is regrettable, Mr. Speaker, because while the methodology of the study is reasonable in part, the Government did not take a very broad look at the issue. The data that it uses is from 1971 to 1981. It is a fact that it takes much longer than 10 years to understand agriculture. Some of the numbers generated in that particular period of time will be highly skewed in a particular direction.
I hope that this study will not be viewed as the Bible on the issue by those members of the committee who make the final decision. I hope they will recognize that some of the land value figures that are used start in 1971, which was one of the most depressed periods of time for agriculture, and end in 1981, which was the time when the peak in agriculture was just coming to an end. I hope the committee will remember that in 1984 preliminary figures show that rather than there being an augmentation in the value of farm assets, we lost between $4 billion and $4.5 billion worth of assets in the value of land and building of Canadian farms. This is because land values are now beginning to taper off. It is estimated that land prices dropped by 16 per cent last year. That was the first year in which we had such a tremendous downturn. It is expected that the downturn in land values will continue in 1985. If the committee makes recommendations based on some of the assumptions in this white paper, which indicates that farm incomes are very good if one takes into account the value of farm assets, the committee will be operating on some very questionable assumptions and will obviously make some wrong recommendations.
However, the data generated some interesting questions. I am sure that it has already been noted that according to the Statistics Canada census there are some 318,000 farms in this country. However, since Section 31 permits farm losses to hobby farmers or those trying to begin a farm operation, when it comes time to file income tax with Revenue Canada sudden-
February 25, 1985

ly there are 450,000 Canadians who claim to be farmers, which is an extra 132,000 farmers recognized as such for income tax purposes. I believe the committee should conduct more research to determine who these farmers are, because the only information we have is from Table 13 of the white paper. It gives us an idea of the type of farmers some of these people are. For example, Table 13 from the white paper points out that 105 of these so called farmers have an average net off-farm income in excess of $400,000. Their farms must be moderate in size because they generate approximately $ 120,000 in sales. While these farmers with large incomes generate an average amount of farm sales it is particularly interesting to note the amount of their average farm loss. In this particular category it is $187,000 as opposed to the $120,000 worth of goods that they produce.
According to Table 13, there are some 1,643 taxpayers who are operating farms essentially to dispose of some of their off-farm incomes. They have off-farm incomes in excess of $100,000 and their farms produce approximately $22,000 worth of gross sales. These farms lose $32,000 each.
It is only when we see the Figures for relatively low off-farm incomes that we get to the category in which the farm is earning more than it is losing. I suggest the committee should review carefully the figures for these farm incomes and farm losses.
The farms of those whose farm incomes are between $25,000 and $35,000 are the farms with greater sales than losses. These are usually young people who are beginning a farming operation. These farms are not being used simply to generate a big loss and avoid income tax. However, it is apparent from the manner in which Revenue Canada has been assessing part-time farmers that it is that lower income group that has given the most trouble. There does not seem to be any problem with so-called farmers whose average off-farm income is in excess of $400,000 but who show a farm-loss of $187,000 on a farm that produces approximately $120,000 of income. Presumably one can obtain a very good accountant with $400,000 of off-farm income in order to continue to write off those losses.
I raise this concern now, even before the committee begins its work, because I do not see any intention on the part of the Government to consider those people with large farm incomes. The Conservatives' campaign promise was to eliminate Section 31, which essentially legitimizes those very large non-farm incomes and permits those operations to take place without any restrictions. Those operations seem to take place in spite of Section 31. It is only those who earn below $35,000 in off-farm incomes who are affected by Section 31.
The question of capital gains tax has been debated in the House a number of times. The study paper rienforces some of the comments I made about the capital gains tax. Let me review those points very quickly. The current capital gains tax regime which permits an in family roll-over enables the very large farms to roll over within the family on a corporate or non corporate basis. These very large farms are able to generate enough farm income to allow the parents to retire without
Tax Issues in Agriculture
taking back their farm investment. That investment can simply be rolled over to the next generation.
Small and middle-income farmers can only retire upon recovering their lifetime investment in order to buy a retirement house and have enough income on which to retire comfortably. Therefore they must get money from the sale of their farm and subject themselves to some form of capital gains tax. The current tax system is inequitable because it has the effect of permitting some classes of farmers to avoid capital gains tax while taxing lower and middle income farmers, just as Section 31 does.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has asked the committee to make some recommendations as soon as four weeks from now. I have grave reservations about its ability to deal adequately with this particular problem in that time, and I merely raise it now so that government Members who will dominate that committee are aware of the present inequities as well as of those that will be created by adopting the white paper recommendation or eliminating the restrictions altogether, according to their campaign promises.
These would have a negative effect on lower and middle-income farmers. I hope the committee will be very sensitive to the special needs of Canada's 318,000 legitimate farmers. We should clearly identify the loopholes which have attracted the approximately 132,000 people who claim to be farmers when it comes time to file income tax.
I think the tax system has failed miserably to carry out the mandate it was given back in 1917 when the then Minister of Finance, Thomas White, said that he hoped the Tax Act would always take account of the difference between what he called "real" farmers who tried to make money and the "fancy" farmers who tried to lose it. I hope that the committee will pay special attention to the 8,200 farms which, for tax purposes, lose vast quantities of money, according to Table 13. Those losses are losses from the pockets of other taxpayers, some of whom are farmers. I hope that those anomalies will be corrected and a proper study can be generated in the few weeks we have to do so.
I am not optimistic that four weeks is enough time. I hope the committee will recommend to the Minister that more time is needed, otherwise farmers will be short-changed. They will have a quick-Fix solution similar to what was offered during the campaign, and that quick-fix solution will affect negatively small and medium-sized farmers who are trying to make a living farming instead of going into farming to show losses so they can avoid tax on their off-farm income.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the debate this afternoon. I am very happy to see that this Order will now be referred to committee. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) made a good point when he said that he wondered why it had taken so long. No doubt a lot of us would have liked to have seen this

February 25, 1985
Tax Issues in Agriculture
issue in committee sooner. Had it not been for the Official Opposition, the Order would have been referred to committee a week ago last Friday and it would have been under way a little sooner. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre makes a good point in that more time is needed. I am sure his comments will be listened to. When we get to committee with the Order, that will be the time to make those comments known.
Let me address briefly some of the concerns raised by the three speakers. First, the official spokesman for the Opposition, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) raises some points to which I would like to respond. He wonders about the position of the Government on this matter. If he looks at the paper put out by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) entitled "A Discussion Paper", on page 1 he will find that it states, "This paper provides information and analysis to assist in consultation on these issues". The three issues are the ones referred to, namely, capital gains, Section 31, and agri-bonds. This paper is exactly what it says, a discussion paper. It is there to provide information and analysis to assist in consultation on these issues. It is nothing more than that. A lot of people would take issue with some of the points raised in the discussion paper. A lot of people would agree with people who take issue with some of the points in the discussion paper. It points out to me, that this Government recognizes that there are some concerns in agriculture and that we are willing to address them.
To be fair about this, we have been in office not quite six months but a number of things have been done. Let me name a few. Two weeks ago we had an Opposition Day on agriculture and many other things were referred to.
Let me outline what has been done. FCC rates were lowered for people in the unfortunate position of having interest on loans as high as 16.75 per cent. Tobacco legislation was put through to allow the tobacco industry, if it chooses, to move a marketing board situation which may help them with problems in marketing. The FCC has set up appeal boards on an experimental basis. They are under way. Very quickly the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) moved to provide drought assistance to livestock producers in the areas in the prairie provinces affected by drought.
Flood agreements were signed with Quebec, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba. The Minister of Finance reduced the tax on farm fuels. Again, a week ago Friday-and I have to thank all the Parties involved-we passed amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act that are very useful. For a Member to stand up and say that this Government has not done anything or does not recognize the problems associated with agriculture, certainly belies the record of this Government so far on agriculture.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext: Contrast that with the Liberals. They did nothing for years.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
The Member from Algoma said, and I think I quote him accurately, that some of these reports are "completely false and won't stand up to the facts". If that is the
case, then we need to have this discussion paper at committee so that the farmers themselves can point out if in fact what the Hon. Member for Algoma says is true. He went on to say that the position as laid out in the discussion paper does not accurately represent the situation. Again, if that is the case, Mr. Speaker, let us hear about it. Let us hear from the farmers, the farm organizations and the groups involved.
It is unfortunate that the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) had to be so strident in some of the comments he was making. It is too bad the Member was not around when the previous Government was in office. He would know, when he is talking about capital gains tax, that it was a Liberal Government in the first place that was responsible for bringing in capital gains tax in 1972.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext: Absolutely right.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext: It is too bad the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is not around now to hear what is going on. I can point out that we do not need to take any lessons on the farming community from the Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell when the Liberal Party does not have one farmer in its caucus. We have a tremendous number of farmers in our caucus. We understand and we will be able to deal as best we can with the problems facing agriculture. I have already pointed out that the Minister of Agriculture has dealt with many of them already. As I said, it was a Liberal Government that brought in capital gains tax in 1972. The Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell would also know that in 1981, after the disastrous Budget of Mr. MacEachen, who is now reposing in another confine in this building, that Government abolished what we call the interest averaging annuity accounts. They were brought in to recognize some of the problems that capital gains tax made in the first place. That was replaced with what was called forward averaging, something no one could understand. Some reasonably knowledgeable mathematicians said that that was one of the most complicated taxation schemes ever designed by man, one that nobody could figure out. This Government's record in five months in terms of what we have done for agriculture should be compared to what the previous Government did, especially regarding capital gains, and I think it is a very unfortunate position for the Member to put himself into.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
When you look back at the last 15, 16, or 17 years of virtually unending Liberal rule, Mr. Speaker, you realize what a disaster that was on the economy. One of the reasons we have so many part-time farmers in Canada who come under Section 31 is the disastrous state of the farm economy which came about as a result of what the previous Government did.
I would say, in referring to the Hon. Member and his comments, that he should at least give us credit for recognizing the problems in the first few months in office and being prepared to deal with them at committee.
February 25, 1985

The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre pointed out that the current system of taxation is inequitable. A lot of people would agree with him. If there are some inequities in the taxation system, and he raised an important one today in Question Period concerning the possibilities of farmers going from a cash system to an accrual system, then let us get this issue to committee and get those things aired and aired by the people who have to live with them every day.
Let me close by making reference to the whole consultation process. One of the reasons so many people in the country are concerned about the consultation process is that they think about it in terms of the previous Government. Whenever they heard anything as a suggestion or a possibility, they always feared the worst because usually that is what they got. They got things without any kind of previous consultation. They got things which they did not necessarily want. They got them without having any input into them. When they see a discussion paper with figures in it which many people do not believe reflect the actual situation, they should take it for what it is- a consultation paper to start the discussion. This does not mean that everything in the paper will end up being part of the recommendation coming from the committee; it simply means that it is a consultation process.
If we think about referring this matter to committee in terms of genuinely trying to hear from the people who will be affected in order to obtain their points of view and to come up with the best possible solution, it is a very useful and helpful way to think about consultation. That is exactly what it is intended to do.
Again I refer to something which was said by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre. There is no doubt that the Government will have the vast majority of Members on the committee. He should take some solace from the fact that many Members on the committee will be either farmers like himself or will have a genuine and very thorough knowledge of the farming industry. That is what we should look at in terms of what comes out of the committee. Those are the people who will be looking at the recommendations. I hope-and at least I can speak for Hon. Members on our side-that the committee will work in a very non-partisan way. For a long time the tradition in this House-and I think it still exists-has been that the agricultural committee functions as one of the most non-partisan committees. It is genuinely interested in the well-being of Canadian agriculture. That committee recognizes how important agriculture is to the whole economy of the country. The best of that showed up a week ago Friday when we put through amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act in one day. That was very much appreciated. It sends out a very healthy, stable and worth-while signal to the farming community in western Canada that there will be an interim payment prior to spring seeding.
There are no legislative impediments. I am assuming that there will be no hold-ups as far as the Senate is concerned. Surely to goodness the occupants of the room for sober second
Tax Issues in Agriculture
thought over there will not see anything wrong with the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I am assuming that they will pass that legislation, but the main point is that it was dealt with very quickly in the House on a non-partisan basis. I appreciate that, as does everyone in the House and the entire farming community in western Canada.
If we can look at referring this discussion paper to the finance committee on that kind of a basis, with the idea that we will do something in the best interests of Canadian farmers from coast to coast on those three issues, it is the proper way to proceed. If more time is needed and that argument is made in committee, I am sure the Minister of Finance will have an open ear. If we deal with it on that basis, not on the basis we heard from the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), many of us in the House will be much better off and will be able to look forward to some worth-while recommendations from that committee to the Minister of Finance.
In conclusion, I thank Hon. Members for referring the matter to the Finance committee. I wish them well in their deliberations and my hope is for speedy recommendation to be made to the Minister of Finance so that he will be in a position to deal with some of them in the coming Budget.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). The response of the House on many Bills has been one of co-operation. For example, I could refer to the National Farm Products Marketing Act relating to tobacco and to the Western Grain Stabilization Act.
The motion before the House was first presented to the Official Opposition about three days before the mid-winter break. Reference was first made to it in the economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 7 or November 8. At that time the House Leader of the Official Opposition told the Government House Leader that we wanted to have a brief debate in the House. We waited for 10 or 11 days, and we still do not have a motion on the Order Paper. We have the motion before us and the matter is under Orders of the Day by unanimous consent, but does the Minister think that dealing with a matter like that and expecting the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to come up with a report in a month is realistic? He is portraying it as if we did not normally put motions on the Order Paper. If we want to make a reference to committee, the proper parliamentary procedure is to place it on the Order Paper. That still has not been done to date. Does he really think that that is co-operation on the part of the Government?
In view of the wording of the motion, is the Government really committed to the campaign promises of abolition of the capital gains tax, of the implementation of a system of agribonds, and of lower interest rates and long-term funding for agriculture? When one reads the white paper, the press reports on it and the motion, one cannot but think that there is a negative attitude toward these issues. The Minister says that

he is keen to hear from farm groups. If my sounding of farm groups is representative of the representations which we will hear from them in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, they will not be very laudatory of this particular white paper.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first comment of the Hon. Member for Algoma, he talked about motions on the Order Paper. What he said is strictly true. Everyone appreciates that by unanimous consent we can virtually do almost anything in the House. Perhaps notice on the Order Paper, as far as the Hon. Member is concerned, would have been more appropriate. However, the important point is that we have it done today. Many times I have had discussions with him in the past on the Western Grain Stabilization Act. As long as there is an attitude and a willingness to co-operate, the most important thing is to get the job done. With regard to whether there is enough time, basically we have five weeks. Certainly more time would be useful and helpful. I do not think anyone would disagree with that, but it is better for us to have five weeks prior to April 1 than no time at all. As I said in reply to the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, if the committee feels that it needs more time, that would be the point at which to decide it and make such views known. Certainly five weeks in terms of hearing the concerns is better than no time at all.
With regard to the third part of his question as to whether we are committed to the three areas-Section 31, capital gains and agri-bonds-the mere fact that we are referring them to committee gives an indication of the Government's intention. To be fair about it, there are also farm groups which are concerned about the removal of capital gains tax and what it can do to the price of farm land. I am not saying whether I agree or disagree with them. However, the point is that there is not unanimity in the farming community. They are concerned, just to make the case which I understand they make, that if we remove capital gains tax we allow people to come in who want to speculate on land and hold it against inflation. That in fact causes problems for people who want to buy land and want to farm it. There are points of view. It is worthwhile during committee stage to take a look at those various concerns. This is exactly what I hope will happen in committee. We will certainly be looking at those three issues in committee.
In conclusion, if we look at some of the things the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) has been doing in terms of the way Section 31 has been administered, I think he is making some strides in having his Department better understand exactly what makes a farmer or what constitutes a genuine farmer and what does not. In my constituency, I know of cases that have been sorted out since the Minister of National Revenue has been there. That has gone a long way, or at least a partial way, in addressing some of the concerns that we have over Section 31.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister. Can we expect a certain amount of backup in the
form of research? For example, 175,000 Canadian farmers are classified as part-time farmers. They lost $619 million, one-third more than the 48,000 full-time farmers. That kind of information is very important. The farmers who are classified in these areas constitute very important information. It is not the kind of information that we as committee members can get.
Can the Minister indicate what kind of research backup we can expect? Could someone from Revenue Canada give us an analysis of that particular issue under Section 31 as to who those farmers are? Do we want to find ourselves in the position of the United States where a section comparable to Section 31 was removed? That resulted in wealthy investors making it a way of losing or getting rid of some of their money for tax purposes. Can we expect considerable assistance?

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF DISCUSSION PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) raises a very valid point. When we go to committee, many of us feel sometimes as if we were captives of the people who are there because we do not have the same kind of background and knowledge. I cannot in good conscience answer the question and say what the committee will or will not be able to do. As the Hon. Member can understand, basically committees are master of their own direction. If we look at the powers available to committees, committees in this House are able to do a lot more things that they are generally believed able to do. There are powers there that committees do not make use of.
In this case, one of the first things the committee will want to do when it convenes is to invite the Hon. Member to put those questions and make those concerns known. I would suspect that he would get a very favourable response. If the committee is going to do a proper and a thorough job, one of the basic things it has to work with is information, particularly the background and the raw data used to compile the discussion paper. I would encourage him to raise this issue at the committee. Based on my knowledge of being in committee and having sat on the committee that looked at the reform of Standing Orders and Procedures in this House, and having some knowledge of the power the committees have and can exercise if they decide to do so, I do not think he would have any problem getting his hands on the information which he refers to in his question.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bissonnette that Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that when we talked about the Small Businesses Loans Act this morning my time had almost expired. I just want to emphasize the problem that I see, especially with regard to outlying areas in this country, under Bill C-23. It will impose an additional service fee on the banks, which will ultimately be reflected in the value of the loan. More important, it will probably reduce the availability of loans for small businesses. I hope the Government will take action to ensure that adequate funding is made available.
No one quarrels much with the interest rates of the small businesses loans, but people do quarrel with the fact that all too often the loans are just not available to small businessmen. I hope the Government does not adopt a policy which will result in a reduction of the amount of loans available. There certainly seem to be two deterrents in the Bill which move in that direction, namely the loan fee and the 10 per cent of the loan guaranteed by the bank. It is very important that the Government take action to ensure that that adverse effect, which we on this side of the House believe will happen, does not happen.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments on the Hon. Member's speech? If not, we will resume debate.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the Hon. Member's speech. I want to assure him that in proposing this legislation this Government has cleared the question of availability of money with the banking institutions. I think the Hon. Member will find in committee that the banking institutions are quite prepared to accept the situation whereby the banks are only guaranteed to the extent of 90 per cent of the loan at a rate of 1 per cent over prime.
In that regard, it is important to put on the record some of the advantages of the Small Businesses Loans Act and how it has progressed over the many years. The House will be aware that this Act was first put forward by the Government led by
Small Businesses Loans Act
the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker in 1960. The first year of operation of the Act was in 1961. The Act has been used by business considerably over the past years, particularly since 1978 when amendments were made to the Act to allow banks to charge 1 per cent over prime.
Last year, the amount of money lent was very close to $1 billion in over 30,000 small businesses loans. Comparing that activity to the activity of the Federal Business Development Bank, Members will note that activity under the Small Businesses Loans Act in terms of numbers of loans was 15 times the activity of the Federal Business Development Bank. This Act and the procedure to finance small business capital requirements has been most successful. The average loan is in the neighbourhood of $25,000, so we are getting at the relatively small, new, starting businesses in this country.
What we are doing under this statute is making it possible for people right across Canada to borrow money to start a business and to buy some equipment. This is not an Act to help large businesses, although the Act does change the situation and allows businesses which have a volume of up to $2 million to take advantage of the statute.
There have been some losses in past years, but they are similar to the losses the banks have suffered generally because we have had problems in the economy, problems with interest rates, problems with insolvencies and so on. We can expect periods like that. In speaking to the small business community, I have found that it is prepared to shoulder its responsibility in terms of paying for the cost of the insurance. Small businessmen can take advantage of a government-insured loan. The small businessmen who cannot get a loan otherwise, are able under this statute to get a loan to buy equipment. We have probably the best system of financing for small business available in any part of the country.
While I think this is an important statute, I am a bit disappointed in the Act as presented. Under the current Act, there is an over-all loan guarantee limit of $1.5 billion, and we have already reached that limit. Indeed, right now it is pretty hard to get a loan under this Act because the limits have been reached. This Bill extends that limit only to $1.8 billion, which I think is too little. I think that is a bit of a failure on the part of the drafters of the Bill. I hope that through discussions in committee the Government will be persuaded to extend that limit. The Government must realize that this has been the most successful form of financing small business.
Members of the committee will obviously take heed of the discussion paper produced by the Minister responsible for small business with respect to financing and the like. Perhaps that discussion paper might be put before the committee.
Sir, this Bill extends the Small Businesses Loans Act for five years. In the past we have had one and two-year extensions, but it seems to me there should be no time limit on the Act. If it should happen that the Act no longer serves the purpose of small business, then it can be terminated. But it seems to me rather ridiculous to continue to put time limits on this Act. It

February 25, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
is time we started realizing that small business is probably going to need some type of long-term financing guarantee now and into the indefinite future. So I recommend to the committee that it seriously consider this question. The Government, influenced by the committee's decisions, might bring forward amendments to alter that portion of the Bill.
As I mentioned already, the total loan guarantee limit of $1.5 billion has now been used up. Therefore, it is important that this debate be terminated and the Bill sent to committee, because we have to make sure that entrepreneurs in this country who want to buy equipment for their businesses are not hamstrung by the fact that this House of Commons cannot get its work done. We have already seen how one portion of Parliament has held up the Government of the country in getting its work done. We have seen that in the borrowing authority Bill. There is no reason why that same thing should happen in this Chamber. Therefore, I say to you, Sir, it is important that this House vote on the Bill and get it into committee where the necessary amendments can be made.
There was a suggestion that the banks should pick up the cost of the guarantee. I suggest to you that a rate of 1 per cent over prime is a very favourable rate. Remember, we are dealing with relatively small loans. The average loan size is about $25,000 up to a maximum of $100,000. All small loans require the same administrative detail as large loans. If a bank lends you $1 million, it does not need any more clerks than it does for a $15,000 or a $20,000 loan. The result is that the overhead on the small loan has to be borne by someone, and I think it is wrong to suggest that, in addition to the 1 per cent margin, the bank be required to pay a 1 per cent insurance fee out of its end. I think small borrowers would be quite prepared to pay a placement fee on a capital loan of this nature, particularly in view of the fact that such fees are common in the industry. If you want to place a long-term loan in the normal course without insurance, you often have to pay a placement fee. A fee of 1 per cent to cover the guarantee is not at all out of line and should be borne by the borrower.
Sir, this Act is working so well that we have used up the maximum amount available. It is working so well that this Parliament should get the Bill before committee so it can be passed and made into law.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to know from the Hon. Member whether, in his constituency, he does not find that the problem with this Act is that there are just not enough loans available. Unless you are a very good friend of the banker, or unless you fit in some pre-selected mould that the banks or credit unions have for their individual customers, there are just not enough loans available. I would be very interested to hear his views on whether, by imposing a 1 per cent charge on the bank, combined with the 10 per cent loss guarantee, the banks will make progress in granting loans.
Clearly, from 1977 to 1984, under the guidance of a strong Liberal Government in Ottawa, except for nine hiccupping months, the number of loans made under this Act went up
from 4,800 a year to some 31,000 a year. Given these two additional conditions, does he really believe that we are going to have as many bankers agreeing to make these loans? Clearly, the Hon. Member has some concerns about his Party's position on the length of this program and he wants to extend it indefinitely. I understood his Party's policy was always to have sunset laws in all Bills, but in any event there is a fibe-year sunset law here and he wants to see it extended indefinitely.
My concern is for the less affluent areas of the country, areas less affluent than the one which the Hon. Member represents and has represented for a number of years. Does he think there is really going to be a large number of loans available under this Act when you impose a 1 per cent fee on the bank as well as require them to assume 10 per cent of all losses under the program?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the Hon. Member that before this Bill was introduced, conversations were held with the major banks in connection with the lending policy with respect to the 90 per cent guarantee instead of the floating 100 per cent guarantee. As the Hon. Member will know, the present guarantee situation is that the banks will not have a 100 per cent guarantee unless the ratio of bank losses is such that it will give them a 100 per cent guarantee. The present system is rather convoluted with respect to guarantees. This legislation has simplified the system so that each loan will be guaranteed to 90 per cent instead of providing a 90 per cent guarantee on a portfolio. I understand that has been discussed with the bankers and that they are quite delighted with it.
With respect to the question of fees, there is some concern which has been expressed by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the Canadian Organization of Small Business. Both of those organizations have consulted extensively with the banking community. Both are convinced that borrowers should pay a placement charge rather than the placement charge being taken out of bank revenues, in view of the narrow revenue which the bank receives. I believe that if that evidence is brought to committee the regulations might well be altered. The regulations must be altered to make that provision.
There is amazing growth in this program. Since the banks were allowed to charge 1 per cent over prime on a floating basis rather than a fixed base, this program Act has grown dramatically. Indeed, this year it amounts to almost $1 billion. The figures in the annual report are quite astounding. The amount of money which has been lent and the number of loans which have been made have grown dramatically.
The Hon. Member said that in some areas small-business people cannot get a loan. I would suggest to him that a loan could be obtained a lot more easily from the banks under the Small Businesses Loans Act than could be obtained from the Government of Canada through the Federal Business Development Bank. The number of loans indicates that the loans are very widespread. Indeed, if the Hon. Member would look at
February 25, 1985

the tables and the financial statements, he would realize how much the loans are spread across the country and how various banks and institutions have taken advantage of the Act in making loans to their customers. There is no reason to believe that this change will affect that situation. However, it will mean that the Government will only be involved as an insurer. The Government is taking an insurance premium to guarantee a loan, the same as the Government takes an insurance premium to guarantee a mortgage under the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There is no reason for business to have a free ride. Indeed, the day of the free lunch is over. Business can afford to pay its cost. The Government is here to assist as an insurer. That is the way it should be. The banks are taking 10 per cent of the risk and the Government is guaranteeing 90 per cent. It will mean that the loans will have to be supervised by the bank in the same way as if it were lending its own money. Because the loans are guaranteed to 90 per cent, we know the banking community will do things that it would not do normally. Certainly, it will lend at a lower rate of interest than it would normally lend, which in this case would be 1 per cent over prime.
I say to the Hon. Member that this is a good statute. It should not be held up by Parliament. It should move to committee as quickly as possible. There are a number of amendments which should be made and I suggest that they can be made as evidence is brought before committee. That is where the legislation should be.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). We support this Bill because we consider it to be a small step in the right direction. However, what will happen if interest rates substantially increase as they did a few years ago? What will be the effect on small business? The loans are being made at 1 per cent over prime, but prime has increased 1.5 per cent in the last few weeks and it is likely that it will increase further in the next few weeks.
In the early 1980s when interest rates were at 18 per cent and 20 per cent, there was a tremendous increase in the number of bankruptcies. The large corporations did not go bankrupt because the banks could not afford to let them go bankrupt. Therefore, the large number of bankruptcies were primarily in the small business sector. What will happen if the prime rate of interest-and therefore the rate of interest which business will have to pay-increases substantially?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) will realize that the prime rate has increased by half a per cent in the past week. That is unfortunate, but it has not increased anything like the underlying rates of interest in Treasury bills, both here in Canada and in the United States. Obviously, we cannot guarantee everyone happiness and prosperity forever. When we realize that Parliament cannot make those guarantees, we will start legislating more for the sensible needs of the country.
It would be nice if we could guarantee fixed-rate lending, but the banking system does not work that way. Depositors
Small Businesses Loans Act
will not invest their money for long periods of time at a fixed rate. They want the current rate on deposit. Therefore, borrowers must pay the current rate on their borrowings. There is no way around it. One per cent over prime is a pretty good rate. I know long-term money can be found. It can be found in the mortgage market at 14 per cent or 14.5 per cent, which is 3 per cent over prime. I suspect we could find long-term business money at 3 per cent or 4 per cent over prime. But businessmen want to borrow money as cheaply as possible. This legislation will let them borrow money at a floating rate as 1 per cent over prime. Whether the Government should guarantee longterm rates on a fixed rate is another matter of consideration. I do not know how we could write the Bill to provide for fixed rate margins, because fixed rate margins are always dramatically higher than floating rate margins.
This legislation is working at 1 per cent over prime. Obviously businessmen like it. The number of dollars which have been borrowed and the number of loans which have been made has escalated dramatically. We ought to support the Bill, get it immediately into committee and, if necessary, make amendments so that it will work even better.

It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand)-Employment-Student	summer jobs-Program
