The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bissonnette that Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Small Busi-

February 25, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
nesses Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleagues have already indicated, we support the Bill because it is a small step in the right direction. We recognize the fact that there are close to one million small businesses in Canada. These businesses are 100 per cent Canadian-owned. They almost always buy from other Canadians and sell to other Canadians. Because they are Canadian, they are interested in seeing their community, their city and their province develop. They are not, like many of the large corporations, particularly the multinational corporations, so determined to make a profit that they will move their business from their community, their city, their province and even from their country in order to receive a substantial increase in profits. In recent years more than two-thirds of all the jobs which have been created in this country have been created by the small business sector.
So it is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that we support this Bill. We recognize that this Bill will make it easier for small business people to get needed funding. While we support the Bill for that reason, we realize that, like other federal legislation which assist farmers and fishermen, this assistance is largely directed toward capital improvements. In effect, it allows small businesses to get into deeper debt in order to continue to operate. It does not necessarily mean they will prosper because they often must compete with far larger corporations with much better access to capital and better tax treatment. Small business people, like the consumers they serve, are largely price takers of the goods and services they require. They do not have the market power to force their own purchase prices on suppliers as do, for example, the large food chains which demand their own volume rebate, which often leaves the farmer in a very bad situation. Instead, these small business people usually pay the going rate and even after they get the kind of credit they need because of this Bill, they will still get hit by inflationary costs. We saw that happen in the early 1980s when interest rates escalated very sharply. Tens of thousands of small businesses were forced into bankruptcy because the premise on which they had based their borrowing and the premise upon which they made arrangements to get loans from the bank, was that much lower interest rates would prevail than those they had to pay two or three years later. So we saw tens of thousands of small business people forced into receivership by the banks as a result of huge increases in interest rates.
It was interesting but sad, to put it mildly, to see the difference in the way the banks treated large corporations as compared to small businesses. There were in past years, Mr. Speaker, and still are today, outstanding, unpaid loans to the bank. These loans are called non-performing loans, that is, loans on which the borrowers pay neither the interest nor the principal, and which today total over $8 billion. Those loans were made almost exclusively to large corporations which borrowed money for takeovers. This added nothing to our
productive capacity and created nothing in the way of jobs. Those loans are still outstanding and in many cases are not even being serviced. Those corporations are not paying interest and are not paying anything on the principal. The reason that the banks are carrying those loans, Mr. Speaker, is that they cannot afford to call those loans in. If those borrowers were required to meet their obligations the financial situation of the banks would be very adversely affected. The banks not only treated the large corporations differently, but they increased the interest rates which the small companies had to pay on their loans. The banks were imposing the kinds of rules on the small companies which frequently forced them into bankruptcy. Banks not only increased the interest rates which small business had to pay but also increased the banks' service charges. In fact, bank charges for the services which they provide have doubled in recent years despite the fact that they have automated and computerized so many of their operations. Banks have recently subjected their smaller accounts to profitability analysis in order to ensure that they make sufficient profit, which will take the form of higher fees or higher service charges.
The Consumers' Association has argued, and, I say, correctly, that these fees should only cover the cost of inducing the consumer to make use of them and that other overheads which are built in should be covered by the spread between the loan and savings deposits rates. Since these charges are often waived at the discretion of the bank, certainly those with the biggest account will wind up getting the best deal. The banks have increased these charges despite the fact that our major domestic banks have operated at profit levels of SI.5 billion or higher in each of the last four years. They have increased these charges despite the fact that other business people have suffered through recessions which have not affected the banks.
We find it interesting that the provisions of this Bill, and other Bills and programs of the Government, bring relatively little benefit to the small business community, certainly as compared to the large corporations of this country. Large corporations have too many friends in important places: the Government, the banks, even public opinion which is manipulated through mass media reporting. For example, in recent years we have seen the Government of Canada ensure that the Chrysler Corporation survived with Government assistance. I am not saying that the Chrysler Corporation should not have been helped, but the fact is that many Chrysler dealerships in that period when the auto industry was in trouble were forced into bankruptcy by the banks. We have seen the Government and the banks carry Massey-Ferguson. I am not suggesing for a moment that the Government should not help important companies which employ large groups of Canadians and which produce products which are needed by Canadians. I am not saying that companies like Massey-Ferguson should not have been helped, but the fact is that Massey-Ferguson dealerships, small business operations, were forced into bankruptcy while the company itself was helped to survive by the banks and the Canadian Government.
February 25, 1985

We believe that small business needs the same kind of support and assistance from Governments which is given to the large corporations, but they do not get that. We have seen large corporations not only receive special assistance, special loans and guarantees-and I am thinking of companies like Dome Petroleum-but we have seen large corporations benefit from a tax system which provides for overly generous deferred corporate taxes. Many corporations in fact pay no real tax at all. Indeed, I believe it was an official of Domtar who, when asked when he thought Domtar would actually pay corporate taxes, replied very simply, "Never". That company is always involved in expanding and improving its facilities, so it pays no corporation taxes. So are small business people, but they are not able to benefit from the deferred corporation tax system we have in this country under which almost exclusively large corporations have now benefited to the extent of $30 billion in deferred taxes which have not been paid.
Similarly, we have permitted a system under which thousands of people with incomes of $50,000 a year or more have simply paid no taxes at all. Indeed, there are more than 250 Canadians with incomes of $250,000 a year who pay no income tax at all. When one compares that with the almost one million small business people who are attempting to get established in a viable small business, we can see the way in which the tax system has been skewed to benefit those who have rather than those who are just beginning.
While we support this legislation, Mr. Speaker, we recognize that of the 900,000 businesses in this country only 25,000 have been or will be helped by this legislation. While this legislation is helpful, it will be seen by some not to provide too much assistance for small business. We are concerned because we believe that this kind of loan system was not really help small business people. Rather, it will make things worse for them if, as happened in the early 1980s, the interest rates on the loans taken escalate very quickly. In that situation those people will be worse off than if they had not received the loan at all.
We have long advocated that the banks of Canada owe it to those who are the source of their profits, to a large extent the small business people of the country, to lend the money at affordable interest rates. That is an interest rate below the prime rate rather than the prime rate plus 1 per cent as provided for in this Bill. That is not a pie-in-the-sky proposal. That is the way in which small businesses are treated in countries such as New Zealand, Denmark and Japan, to mention only a few. In those countries small businesses are able to borrow money at less than the prime rate. They are able to do that for a number of years, particularly in the start up years when they are working the hardest to establish themselves.
We believe that the Bank Act should be amended to force the chartered banks to lend money to small businesses at rates comparable to those offered to big corporate borrowers. We believe that there should be more real risk and venture capital
Small Businesses Loans Act
provided for small business people. We believe that the Federal Business Development Bank should provide more money to small businesses at lower interest rates. We believe that there should be a more aggressive buy Canadian program. Government tendering practices have to be reformed. The Government of Canada and the provincial Governments are among the biggest purchasers of goods and services in the country. Their system of purchasing should be changed to encourage small businesses to participate in supplying the needs of governments. If that were done, if we had a real buy Canadian program and encouraged small business to participate in that program, a big part of the ability of small business people to survive and grow would be realized.
We believe that the corporate tax system should be reformed so that small businesses will not be forced to pay a higher effective tax rate than large corporations, which they are now required to do. We believe that small business people cannot survive and grow in this country unless we have an independant Canadian interest rate policy. That policy would dramatically cut the cost of borrowing for the average small business person by ensuring that the Bank of Canada rate is no more than 1 per cent above the rate of inflation. We pride ourselves on the fact that the interest rate is down dramatically. It is not at 20 per cent or more as it was a few years ago. However, if one looks at the spread between the rate of inflation and the interest rate, we see that the real interest rate is almost as high as when it was at 20 per cent plus.
We believe that we must protect the Canadian dollar from the kind of swings which are taking place right now, fueled in part by speculators. We need to protect the Canadian dollar by coupling an independent interest rate policy with a tax on speculative capital leaving the country. That speculative capital is not leaving the country because small business people are involved in that kind of speculation. They are too interested in just surviving to get involved in that kind of thing.
We need more than just this Bill which we are discussing today, Mr. Speaker. We need to work for changes in the Bank Act which will require the banks to lend a Fixed percentage of their money to homeowners, farmers, and small business people at the same rate as that enjoyed by big corporate borrowers. We are going to support this Bill, but we think it goes only a small way to meeting the needs of the small business community. We believe that unless the Government can divorce itself from American fiscal policies, and unless we can get a lower and stable interest rate, small business people will not get real benefits from this Bill but will, rather, suffer all the evil consequences they suffered in recent years when interest rates were very high and swinging up and down very quickly.

Mr. Speaker, one of the clauses in the Bill imposes a user fee on the small business borrowing with the guarantee of the Small Businesses Loans Act. Would the Hon. Member comment on that particular clause? Does he think it is worth-while, or should we be attempting to remove it at committee stage?

February 25, 1985
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act

Mr. Speaker, 1 think the important question which must be resolved is whether the user fee is going to inhibit the borrower or the banks from extending the loans which are required. 1 think we must hear representations from the small business community and the banks before we make a final decision as to what we should do about that user fee.

speechtext: Is there unanimous consent for the House to proceed to Item No. 136?
Agreed.

That the Standing Committee on Agriculture be empowered to study and report on the advisability of amending the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, to allow expansion of the Act into a National Farm and Forest Rehabilitation Act which would administer co-ordination of national action with respect to both wet and dry-land management; and making the Minister responsible for the consideration and implementation of the best methods to be adopted to secure the rehabilitation of farm and forest areas throughout Canada; and bring new technology into the hands of individual farmers and foresters and to coordinate national action with respect to drought/water/soil management as well as conservation, wet-lands management (including wildlife preservation), and the general enhancement of the quality of our rural heritage; and that the Administration of the National Farm and Forest Rehabilitation Act be granted the power to make, administer and supervise farm and forest loans to help operators recover from natural disaster conditions and that such loans be granted at reduced rates of interest for short periods of time to ensure rapid restoration of the operations in question.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to see so many Members in the House today. I have been a Member in the House for some 13 years and it is because I have such a high regard for Private Members' motions that I have put forward this motion. As well, I have such high regard for the good work that the standing committees have been able to do that rather than recommend that the Government take this motion into consideration, I have recommended that the Standing Committee on Agriculture take into consideration the revision of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
This organization has been in place for almost 50 years and has served the prairie farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta honourably over those years. It has built an excellent reputation among the rural communities of the Prairies.
When it began in the 1930s, it dealt with drought and soil erosion. It moved on to provide guidance on irrigation, shelter belts and new farm practices that have served the rural communities in the Prairies very well.
It is my intention that the standing committee look at this organization after 50 years of service to see whether now is the time to expand it so that its expertise can be used in other regions in the country.
Soil erosion is not just common to the Prairies. The Senate committee has pointed out that soil erosion is now a problem in the whole country and something about which we should be concerned. As well, it has the ability to study wet-land management, as this organization has been involved in the drainage of areas and the establishment of shelter belts to encourage wildlife sustenance in the prairie region.
I have been advised that the expertise could also be used in the management of small woodlots and shelter belts across the country. It is my intention, and I hope that of the House, that we pass this motion to the Agriculture Committee for study and recommendation to the Government for action.
Let me elaborate on some areas that I think the committee should study. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act should be changed to reflect the national perspective. I suggest that it be called the National Farm and Forest Rehabilitation Act. Its mandate should be expanded to include water management and conservation throughout Canada and soil conservation and management. Soil deterioration and degradation is still a very serious problem in this country and is costing us hundreds of millions of dollars.
The present Act should be expanded to include forest management specifically concerned with the preservation of small woodlots such as the maple sugar woodlots that are operated by small entrepreneurs. It would not in any interfere with the management of our large forests for which the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) is responsible.
This organization, which is already working in co-operation with Ducks Unlimited, should become involved in wet-lands management, including wildlife and particularly waterfowl management. It should revive the cultural aspects of rural life that it was originally set up to include. I suggest that policies that are established to enhance rural life be part of the work of
February 25, 1985

this organization, along with soil and water management. The PFRA allowed that aspect to diminish as it dealt more with the research aspect of agriculture. However, Agriculture Canada has allowed that aspect to slip as well as a result of its concentration on new crops and crop management over the years. 1 think it is important to revive the cultural aspect of the Act.
I hope that the PFRA can be expanded to administer farm and small woodlot loans to help operators recover from natural disasters by obtaining low interest loans. We experienced such a disaster in the Prairies this year. Although the Governments of the provinces and the federal Government responded reasonably quickly, I believe it is important to have an organization of Government that can respond immediately to a natural disaster, no matter how large or small. I hope that an organization such as the one that is proposed could have that opportunity.
It is important that we do not leave the impression that by moving this motion we are taking anything away from the Prairies. The prairie provinces are very proud of this institution and do not want to have its importance in that region of the country diminished. Therefore, I believe that it is important to have the support for this suggestion of the Departments of Agriculture in the Prairies and of the prairie Premiers. It is my opinion, after talking to the staff in PFRA, that they would welcome this new challenge and welcome the new guidelines to take them into the next 50 years of operation.
I believe there are available the co-operation and ability necessary to permit this organization to expand into regions other than the Prairies if those regions wish to use that expertise. It would only be done on that basis so that we do not in any way encourage the centralization of this organization. If there is a need for this expertise, it should be expanded on a regional basis so that we in no way diminish the importance of the organization that was built up to which there was such good response on the Prairies.
This organization presently has a trained and capable staff. I believe that it would not be necessary to have a large increase in staff since it already has the potential to expand its work load and provide that expertise. In fact, some expertise could be borrowed from other government Departments to meet certain requirements at particular times, with the exception of the natural disaster aspect of the program. It would not require a large increase in staff. We now have existing in this organization a silviculture operation at Indian Head, Saskatchewan. It has been very successful in dispersing trees capable of lining property lines, enhancing the farm, homestead, or the farmstead of an entrepreneur. This program and the people who have been part of establishing this program are in place. This expertise is available not only to the Prairies but it could be made available to other areas.
I anticipate the maritime region of Canada and British Columbia would be very interested in having assistance from this organization. As I said before, the PFRA has not in the
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
strictest sense been involved in wet-land management in the past. It has been involved directly in drainage programs and in taking farm land out of production which should ever have been in production in the first place and re-establishing it into community pastures or back to its natural state. I believe this is an area into which PFRA could expand, to assist in the preservation of wildlife with the co-operation that is in place with Ducks Unlimited. They have the experience in establishing dug-outs and in establishing shelter belts. This kind of management is very important to the natural wildlife of many regions, particularly the Prairies. There is a natural ability to expand in these areas if we find a need.
I believe this program should be studied intensively. I believe the Standing Committee on Agriculture has the ability to do that. We are not suggesting that it be passed and implemented tomorrow but that we look at the positive aspects of making this a national organization. I anticipate that we should take some time to do that and we should not rush into establishing a new mandate for an organization that has operated very well in the past.
As far as the natural disaster aspect of the proposal is concerned I believe a dire need exists in Canada today. If we look at our neighbour to the south, the United States of America, we find that it has had in place for some time an organization called the Farmers Home Administration. It has the ability to lend funds for a short period of time to farmers who find themselves the victims of natural disasters. These loans are only for emergencies. Farmers can receive loans at interest rates of 5 per cent on the first $100,000 and 8 per cent on the remainder. Loans are limited to $500,000. They must be repaid as quickly as possible or turned back into the established credit arrangements as quickly as possible. This allows the farmer to secure cash quickly at low rates in order to recover from a natural disaster. I would like to see the same kind of assistance offered to our farmers in rural communities who may find themselves victims of such things as tornadoes.
We never had such things as tornadoes in Canada at one time but we have had three or four in my constituency in the last five years. Weather patterns are changing and natural devastation is a possibility. We have lived with drought for many years. This is the reason for this organization to be established. As a Member of this House I suggest we seriously look at increasing the mandate of this excellent organization that has been successfully established on the Prairies for 50 years. We should expand its mandate to the entire country and allow the expertise that has been built up to be used by Canadians no matter where they are participating in rural life.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schel-lenberger) in speaking on his motion this afternoon. It relates to a proposal to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for the ideas behind his motion. Of all the issues facing agriculture in the long term, the whole issue of conservation and soil degradation, will perhaps be the most important in the future. That is not in any way to discount the short-term problems of marketing, of the

mentioned that the utilization of conservation practices by the majority of farmers could be encouraged by the availability of more funds through programs which are seen to be fair and non-restrictive. Cost-sharing programs, tax credits and capital cost allowances were the most frequently proposed incentives in the hearings the committee held across the country, while it was suggested that other financial assistance measures should be carefully studied.
What we have to consider in the motion today is whether or not we really have a Government which is prepared to provide that kind of financial assistance, in view of the response to the debt crisis facing some 17 per cent to 20 per cent of our farmers and the move to put half the cost of disaster funding on to the agricultural producers of the country, while not requiring the provinces to make any commitment at all. What we are really asking is whether there is the political will to implement a program such as the one the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin has put before us. If there is, obviously the exercise of a committee report would be very beneficial from that point of view. We should move ahead with it and see it go to committee. Those of us who represent rural areas know that the rural farm population represents only 4 per cent or 5 per cent of the total population. Obviously it is not a very loud voice in the over-all spectre of political power, yet this issue is very fundamental to the long-term benefits of the rural areas of Canada.
During the years I worked as a veterinarian in western Canada and then in northern Ontario and for the past 16 years as a Member of Parliament working in the rural areas of the Algoma, Manitoulin and Sudbury districts of northern Ontario, I have certainly had a chance to see the very serious problems facing agriculture. There is a need to impress upon the Government the fact that there should be a commitment to rural areas. I would like to see as part of the Hon. Member's motion mention of the quality of life, general development and a commitment to rural areas.
In the Senate committee report Soil at Risk, one of the main items was that there be on the agenda of the meeting of First Ministers' soil conservation and soil degradation. A First Ministers' conference was held in Regina a week or so ago. Clearly that item was not there. That does not mean that we should not move ahead as a committee of the House to try to deal with this motion to see if a national program can be fashioned to meet the needs recognized in the Senate committee report and determine whether there is a commitment by the Government to implement such a policy. Clearly there is a need.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate to discuss the proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) to refer to the Standing Committee on Agriculture the power to study the amendments to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. He has a number of proposals that that administration might carry on as part of its expanded
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act mandate. During the course of my remarks, I would like to add to such an expanded mandate one or two other items that I think might be legitimate.
It is an extremely important topic both for Canadians and other residents of North America and we should address this problem now. With its advent in the 1930s, the PFRA showed that it was able to bring back some land that had gone beyond use. Some of the lands that were brought back into production were, granted, as grass-lands and pasture lands. They had degenerated to the point where they were little more than sand dunes. The activities of PFRA brought those back.
Vast areas of the Prairies that were devoid of any water, through the actions of PFRA had small dams and drainage systems installed. Fair amounts of water were trapped for the use of the human population, the livestock and waterfowl that passed through that region. It may not be well known in the rest of Canada, but most prairie people know that approximately 50 per cent of the waterfowl that exists in North American migrate through the prairie region. Approximately 50 per cent of that waterfowl are hatched, grow up and become usable as birds for the hunt in that part of the country.
I have noted a number of disturbing things that are happening to the wet-lands, woodlots and farm-lands of our country. The problems have not been adequately addressed, in part because of our Constitution where the responsibility lies with both the federal and provincial jurisdictions. The genius of PFRA was the fact that it succeeded in getting provincial and federal co-operation and that it channelled the job that needed to be done through that particular administration.
The Hon. Member who introduced this motion is absolutely right. We need to have an expanded and new mandate for either PFRA or some new administration which would have both federal and provincial co-operation and financing. It could be mandated by both federal and provincial governments. We should not rule out the possibility of financing from our neighbours to the south since a great deal of the benefits from the wildlife, and certainly from the water and fisheries, shifts to them.
If we properly manage our forest lands so that the silt from the mountains stops washing into the rivers, the salmon beds will be clean. We can again have salmon using the rivers and hatching. We will again get to the point where we will have full utilization of all the fishboats on both our coasts. We will not have the continuing argument and litigation between our two countries as to who is fishing how many salmon and who is responsible for dividing the salmon. We have allowed our forests to deteriorate to the point where our spawning grounds for those salmon are no longer capable of supporting fish.
I alluded briefly to the role that the Prairies play in supplying waterfowl for both nations. We sometimes forget the problems in attempting to save our waterfowl, forests, fisheries or the land over-all. It is a very complex question. Our farmers and foresters look after the land as they see fit by the rules that they have to work by. Sometimes, while they may be doing things that are considered to be very good management for their particular industry, the long-term effect may be very

February 25, 1985
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
expensive for the rest of us. We always have the question as to who will pay the cost of conservation. We can get general agreement that conservation is good for this and future generations, but when it comes to who will lay out the money or who will put up with the problems that accrue when you try to conserve natural resources, that is something we have not be able to address properly. In part, that is because of the split jurisdiction. There are other problems, some of which I will allude to.
As an example, I will take my own area. Most of us are most comfortable talking about our own area. Where I live in Saskatchewan, the land was originally covered by fairly heavy forests, poplar and spruce. Underneath the good forest was some very good farm land. Otherwise, it would not have produced good forest. For three generations, farmers in my corner of the country have considered themselves successful if at the end of the year they could say they have cleared so many acres. We fought the forest, got rid of it and have now turned it into farm land. That is considered a measure of success.
We have reached the point now where most of the farm land is clear. A lot of fencelines were left, growing up into tall trees, which slowed down the winds both in summer and winter and provided habitat for some of the smaller wildlife, including deer. As farmers began to use larger and larger equipment and were pressed economically, they began to look at those fencelines as if they were enemies rather than friends.
The farmers began to pull out the fencelines. It does not cost much to knock down a mile or a mile and a half of fenceline. They found that they could get on their fields two or three days earlier than their neighbours who had left the fencelines up. They had no birds and no wildlife. However, they were a couple of days earlier and they avoided the frost. It did not take long for the neighbours to see that the "successful farmer" did not keep tree lines. So my part of the country, which was once verdant with trees, is now laid bare, and you can see a distance of five or six miles just as though you were on the Prairies. Of course, the winds blow through and the snow does not stop in the middle of the fields and we are having attendant problems with water in the spring. The snow melts very quickly, creating erosion as it goes. Some farmers consider that erosion helpful because it clears out the water courses and allows the water to escape even more quickly so that they can get their crop in a few days earlier. But in the longer term the next generation in that part of the country may find themselves faced with a shortage of water. We know from experience on the Prairies during the 1930s that once you dry out the land too much, the rains stop coming. We may be having some influence on the weather patterns in that part of the world. In the long term it may be a very costly exercise of these very efficient farmers to have made the best economic use of their resources.
We know from observing monoculture, not only in our region but in other regions, that the results can be quite
hazardous in a period of only 10 or 15 years. Sometimes it takes as long as one or two generations, but the result is always quite visible. I know from having visited the single-crop potato area of New Brunswick that erosion is a much larger problem there than it is even on the Prairies. The water courses wash great gouges in the soil each spring. They are filled in, planted over, no fibre is put back into the soil and the process continues again the next year. We have no way of saying to farmers that these water courses should be seeded with grass to hold them in place. We have no agency which could point out the advantages of keeping trees as part of the ecology of our farm areas. We have no one selling the advantages of trees except for some people who are now getting old, having started out back in the thirties. They did a good job of explaining why we needed tree-lines and trees on the Prairies, but the message did not sink in, not in those areas where there were trees to begin with, and we now seem to be doomed to making the errors that our prairie farmers made.
In his motion, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin has set out to have the new farm and forest rehabilitation agency co-ordinate national action with respect to both wet and dry-land management. He wants new technology placed in the hands of individual farmers and foresters, and I think some environmentalists and wildlife managers as well. Along with that- and perhaps this agency is the one to do it-there has to be an organization to do genuinely innovative research, an organization that would investigate quite new ideas, some which might be considered to be whacky, but which might have an impact on the over-all environment.
To give you one example of that, Mr. Speaker, most Members of the House will realize that there is a big salinity problem in a lot of prairie soils. We do not have anyone who has done anything more than just determine that if you keep plants growing on those saline spots, the problem gets somewhat better. Farmers have noticed that if you just abandon those areas in some parts of the Prairies to the kochia weed, gradually the area seems to shrink in size and again become available for agricultural production. The suspicion is that this weed may have some ability to reduce the amount of salt in those areas, but there is no one doing research to identify that.
I know, for instance, that there has been research in similar areas which has arrived at surprising results. The National Research Council had a research centre in Saskatchewan some six or eight years ago, when I was on the Science Council of that province, that had done some research with cattails and bullrushes. They found that those particular shallow-water plants had the uncanny ability to take heavy metals out of sewage and sludge, both in the water and in the soil, and seemingly get rid of it from the environment. At the same time, they produced a plant which was usable for livestock feed. I think that that researcher should be tracked down and he should do some similar work on the kochia weed, which seem to be able to absorb some salt from the saline spots which are a growing problem on prairie soils.
Another proposal is to have a research unit do truly innovative research which our plant breeders and agriculturalists
February 25, 1985

cannot get the money to do. This would have an effect on the over-all ecology of our country and would improve the management of our wildlife.
I should not have to remind the House, but some may have forgotten, that our fur industry, which started this country, is still a very important industry. It is considered a sideline perhaps more than it should be. Approximately $900 million worth of furs are taken by trappers and farmers and they provide a sizeable addition to the income of people who live in forested areas. There is, as well, the management of our water resources in order to assist in the growth of migratory wet-land birds. That should be part of the authority as well, because it contributes markedly not only by way of meat for native hunters, but it is also a very large draw to the tourist industry and it can be one of the larger industries in the more remote parts of our country.
I think the idea is a good one and its scope could be extended beyond the very broad terms of reference that the Hon. Member has presented to us. I would be quite pleased to see this idea go to committee for further study, and our Party will support it.

Mr. Speaker, in the report prepared by the Senate entitled "Soil at Risk", the authors described the state of agricultural soil across Canada. They point out that soil degradation is a serious problem throughout the country. Although there are some similarities, there are enough differences from region to region to require specific corrective action.
Soil management must deal with the problems of erosion and compaction caused by potato farming in the Maritimes, with floods and erosion by water in Quebec and Ontario, with salinization and erosion by water and wind in the Prairies and water erosion and river sedimentation in British Columbia. Widely differing problems require as many different solutions.
The time has come for the Government of Canada to review its activities with respect to soil, forests, waterways and wet lands, and the preservation of our rural heritage. It is clear that the end of the eighties and the beginning of the nineties mark the beginning of an era when developing the land and nothing more will no longer be acceptable. We will have to manage the resources we have to ensure our economic and general well-being.
Our water resources are unevenly distributed among the various regions. Ontario and Quebec often suffer from problems caused by spring floods or torrential rains. Soil erosion is one of the most serious problems, and the increase in row crops such as corn makes a serious situation even worse. In some areas, it costs between $100 and $600 per hectare to correct these conditions.
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
Another example, and I am still referring to central Canada, is that wind erosion is getting worse on sandy soil because of a movement away from cover crops to single crop culture.
And what about soil compaction as a result of repeated plowing in wet soil? This could be just as damaging as flooding and erosion, depending on the area.
Urban expansion in Ontario has meant that agriculture is losing its best arable land. The same phenomenon exists, to a lesser degree, in the Maritimes. In Quebec, strict zoning laws applied since the end of the seventies have helped stop excessive urban expansion, but good farmland remains a rare and high-priced commodity. In the Prairies, water is a particularly unreliable resource, and it has always been difficult to remedy this problem.
Canada's economic development depends on control and effective use of our water resources. Increased use puts greater pressure on our water supply and increases the probability of pollution. Only through effective management and use can we ensure long term availability of our water supply.
When we travel across this country of ours, we can see the incredible diversity of our forests and how they contribute to the well-being of local communities: woodlots and maple bush in the East, the pulp and paper industry in Quebec and Northern Ontario, and British Columbia's vast forest resources. Over the years, we have developed forest resources across this country. Our forests must provide sustained production if we want them to continue to contribute to our prosperity and wellbeing. We should develop and implement a new technology aimed at encouraging conservation, developing reforestation and promoting a more effective management.
Wetlands also play a major role. Compared with the economic roles of our agriculture and forests, that of wetlands is more germane to our environment, way of life, culture and heritage. These areas contribute to the maintenance and enhancement of water quality, the preservation of wildlife habitat, as well as the development of tourism through outdoor activities such as hunting, fishing and nature interpretation centres. They attract those who are eager to educate themselves and contribute to the ecological diversity of our landscapes. They play a part in flood control by holding back the water in times of heavy rainfalls and allowing it to flow during the following months. And they are the depositories of a great many renewable resources such as fur animals and wild rice.
Many wetlands have been drained or greatly modified through the development of up-stream basins. Canadians are becoming increasingly more aware of the extensive damage resulting from the interference with the ecosystems within wetlands. These must be preserved, given the part they play in the use of lands.
Soils, forests, water, humid zones and people are all part and parcel of our rural heritage. The agricultural community

February 25, 1985
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has found ways to protect and improve the environment, be it through upgrading farms by tree-planting, maintaining ecosystems to protect wildlife, or furthering its cultural charateristics to make rural life more rewarding. Communities are part of that heritage and the quality of their social life must be improved.
What is the common link between those natural resources? The provinces look after their development because it is their constitutional responsibility.
Besides, the federal Government has a direct interest in those fields. Soils and forests do contribute to our international trade. Agriculture accounts for one-sixth of all Canadian economic activities. Last year, retail sales of food products were worth nearly S60 billion. In 1983, agricultural exports were valued at $10 billion and boosted our trade surplus by $4.3 billion. This industry directly employs 1.4 million Canadians and creates 3 million jobs all told.
The forest industry ranks first in export trade since it brings in over $11 billion each year. It directly employs more than 300,000 Canadians and indirectly about 700,000 additional workers in related industries.
The federal Government has every interest in making sure that those resources are properly administered since they stand as a guarantee of economic stability and jobs for future generations. The provinces as well as all men and women who use those resources share the same interest. We have seen to what extent the quality of such resources can vary from one region to the next, and that explains why each provincial Government has developed its own management strategy in those fields.
In the past, the federal Government has launched a variety of programs. Research has always been a priority with respect to soils, forests and water. Now and again, it has also involved the provinces through short-term financing programs under the Agricultural and Rural Development Act, through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or again, more recently, through regional and economic development agreements. In addition, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration (PFRA) plays an active role in Western Canada as a federal body which provides direct services.
It is imperative that we foresee our needs for 1990 and years beyond, decide what must be done and how to do it. So far, we have been acting as we saw fit, but time has come to make sure that our resources produce sustained yields through more effective administration.
Mr. Speaker, I am looking at the clock and I feel that Hon. Members are getting nervous. We have very little time left and we do want this motion to be adopted, convinced as we are that action must be taken in those fields. We support the motion to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. We are anxious to hear its recommendations and, if need be, to make the right decisions and take the appropriate steps.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is the House ready for the question?

It has been moved by Mr. Schellenberger, seconded by Mr. Nickerson:
That the Standing Committee on Agriculture be empowered to study and report on the advisability of amending the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, to allow expansion of the Act into a National Farm and Forest Rehabilitation Act which would administer co-ordination of national action with respect to both wet and dry-land management; and making the Minister responsible for the consideration and implementation of the best methods to be adopted to secure the rehabilitation of farm and forest areas throughout Canada; and bring new technology into the hands of individual farmers and foresters and to co-ordinate national action with respect to drought/water/soil management as well as conservation, wet-lands management (including wildlife preservation), and the general enhancement of the quality of our rural heritage; and that the Administration of the National Farm and Forest Rehabilitation Act be granted the power to make, administer and supervise farm and forest loans to help operators recover from natural disaster conditions and that such loans be granted at reduced rates of interest for short periods of time to ensure rapid restoration of the operations in question.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?
Agreed.
Motion agreed to.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 45 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-STUDENT SUMMER JOBS-PROGRAM ANNOUNCEMENT. (B) SCOPE OF PROGRAM

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on February 5, for the third time in this House, I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) when she would announce the summer employment program. I asked that question in December, in January and also in committee. I pointed out to the Minister that it was customary to announce the summer employment program in December in order to give enough lead time to potential employers and applicants so that they could put together worth-while programs to hire students in the summer.
When I asked the Minister a third time on February 5, she said that the program would be announced the next day. In fact, the program was announced on February 6.
I might say that the two-month delay in announcing the program did not give justice to the program because, while it was worth $205 million, as a result of the rate of inflation it would be worth less real money than in the previous year, and it had no specific allocation for community services. It also
February 25, 1985

had a different name, I suppose because the Conservative Party, after delaying for two months, wanted to put its own stamp on it. Instead of calling it "Summer Canada", it was called "Challenge '85".
When the Minister announced the program on February 6, she gave the impression that the program was ready to proceed. I am raising this matter again today because she misled the House on that date. When the Minister announced the program on February 6 she gave a certain number of details, and we had the impression on that date that finally the program was ready to go ahead. However, as of last week- two and a half weeks after the announcement-the program was still not ready.
It had not been decided by many of the provinces whether the program would be a joint program, or that there would be two separate programs, federal and provincial. As well, the provincial insert sheets for the application forms were not ready for potential applicants. Furthermore, the deadlines and the selection processes were not clear. For example, last Friday I was told by one of the officials of the Department of Employment and Immigration in Montreal that the program would be constituency based. But another official from another office told me that it was going to be regionally based.
This is another example of Conservative incompetence, Mr. Speaker. The Government cancelled the Summer Canada Program on November 8. It bumbled and fumbled for three months. Finally it announced a program on February 6 even though it was not ready, and it was not ready because the details had still not been worked out. I presume that the announcement of February 6 was simply to put off people like myself and other Hon. Members who have been asking the question over and over again, "When are you going to announce that program?" I called again today and I was told that finally the application forms are being sent out to the people in the Montreal area. I don't know what the experience is in other parts of the country but I am told that in Toronto last week they still did not have the Ontario insert forms for the application forms. It is regrettable, Mr. Speaker, that the Government, having played politics with this matter, now leaves students holding the bag.
I must say that my complaint is not so much against the program but against the process, against the administration. During the election campaign the Conservative Party gave the impression that it had all of the answers to unemployment in this country and that if the Conservatives were elected those problems would be solved. Once the election was over, the Conservatives announced that they were going to consult with that group, or this group, with the provinces, with labour, with big business, with little business and with community groups and so on. It then became fairly evident that they were looking for a program. If the Conservatives had said that in the first place, before the election, we would have accepted that as reasonable. But, no, they gave the impression that they had the answers and then started looking for the answers; in effect, trying to reinvent the wheel.
Adjournment Debate
In a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 8 cancellation of Summer Canada was announced. It was later announced that the Government was going to look for a new program, or consult on a new program. The new program was finally announced on February 6, two months late. It would have been bad enough had the program started from that date but, as I pointed out, it is just now getting ready. I feel that is a terrible condemnation of the Government on its approach to the very serious problem of unemployment among our students.
Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that despite these unpardonable delays, the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary, and those who support the Government, will listen to these pleas, not only from the Opposition, as we are only 70 in number, but from the many student groups and community groups across the country. The government should finally get this summer program fully under way as soon as possible to make sure that students are working by at least May 1, 1984 in order that they can earn enough money to pay for their tuition and other expenses next year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-STUDENT SUMMER JOBS-PROGRAM ANNOUNCEMENT. (B) SCOPE OF PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), I would like to respond to the question asked by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) in this House on February 5, 1985, concerning the announcement made by the Government of its summer employment program for the young, and to his request for information on the nature of those initiatives.
On February 6, 1985, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of State (Youth), (Mrs. Champagne) announced the program Challenge '85, a summer employment program for students, with a $205 million funding. That program should not only give students an opportunity to earn money to pay for their tuition fees, but also create jobs that will promote their career goals and a better preparation for their future participation in the labour market.
The Hon. Member is under the impression that the delay in announcing the program is a serious insult to the Canadian students. On behalf of the Minister, I would point out that any program hastily introduced, without specific planning, without input from the regions and without taking the time needed to obtain a commitment from our economic partners, including the Provinces, the private sector and others, would be a still more serious insult.
Challenge '85 is a totally new approach to job creation for students. Instead of offering students pre-organized federal projects that would simply give them an opportunity to earn money to pay for their tuition fees, we in the Government are challenging our economic partners to work with us for the creation of meaningful jobs that will enable students to opti-

February 25, 1985
Adjournment Debate
mize their contribution both to the Canadian society of today and that in which they will be living in the years to come.
Challenge '85, a multisided initiative, illustrates the Government's conviction that the students of Canada and our economic partners have the ingenuity, the desire and the will needed to carry on a successful program, and that they can very well at the same time play their rightful role in rebuilding a healthy Canadian economy.
Challenge '85 will provide $163 million for the Summer Employment/Work Experience component. With respect to that component, the federal participation will take the form of wage subsidies for jobs not only in the private sector but also in municipal goverments and community service organizations.
In all these sectors, priority will be given to applicants offering jobs to students while giving them the opportunity to acquire more knowledge, job experience and training in a future career. Mr. Speaker, this should alleviate the fears of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East that groups such as community non-profit organizations will be left out next summer. Our second priority will be for jobs where students will be able to acquire some work experience.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government in cooperation with the provinces is willing to make $30 million available in the form of loan guarantees and loans for those wishing to go into business.
The Minister sent out an invitation to large corporations and business organizations, which have already suggested that they would gladly promote student hiring in the private sector.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would like to mention that, with this program and the involvement of the provinces and the private sector, the Government is confident that Challenge '85, an inspired and audacious new approach to student hiring, will be of great help to thousands of students both next Summer and in the near future when they will enter the labour market for good.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REVIEW OF PROGRAMS. (B) AGENDA OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
AGRICULTURE-REVIEW OF PROGRAMS. (B) AGENDA OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 14 I put a question to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) who had made a very grand presentation to the Canadian Club of Toronto about two days before that. On that occasion in his speech entitled "Agenda for Change", he outlined study teams in the various sectors of the Canadian economy whose job it was to cut out, eliminate, reduce and consolidate programs. I asked him why there was no representation on the study team on agricultural programs from the agricultural community itself, that is agricultural producers and farmers. I asked him why there was no representation from eastern or western Canada. I asked why was there no representation from rural Canada, and why was there no
representation from women involved in the agriculture industry?
When you look at the study team you will see that most of its members are from multinational corporations, banking institutions or the federal Government. The team leader is a past president of St. Lawrence Sugar. The private sector people come from the large multinational corporations or banks. The other five come from the Public Service. Surely it would have been reasonable to expect that there would be representation from western Canada on a study team that will be reviewing some 90 Government programs relating to agriculture, programs which involve some 14,000 jobs and an expenditure of $1.5 billion. Surely there should be some such representation.
The response from the Deputy Prime Minister was that the private sector advisory committee members are broadly representative of all regions of this country, business and labour. That is totally wrong. It is questionable whether the Deputy Prime Minister read his own speech. When he was replying to a question by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) he did not seem to know what he said in his speech. It is as if he just read the speech without really understanding what he was saying.
I fear for the agricultural community. Let us look through the list of programs. It seems to me that on the committee studying livestock and farm input supply there could have been a livestock producer from western Canada or eastern Canada. Having regard to programs such as the Seed Potato Export Promotion Program, one might consider having a representative from New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island on the committee.
Rather than having this collection of people from Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa consider programs under the Agricultural Products Co-Operative Marketing Act, it seems to me there should have been members from co-ops in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or elsewhere on the committee. That would be more sensible than having a few former presidents of big multinational corporations and some civil servants deciding which Government programs will be maintained.
It is most disturbing to find upon reading the published documentation that the committee has already made its report. The interim report apparently was made on February 15, two days after the Deputy Prime Minister made his fateful speech to the Canadian Club in Toronto. It would have been interesting if he had made that speech to the Canadian Club in Winnipeg. I have a press clipping from Manitoba which is highly critical of the Deputy Prime Minister. Not only was there no representative from Manitoba on the study committee on agricultural programs, there was no such representation on any of the approximately 12 committees the Deputy Prime Minister set up. I am sure that in response to every program that gets chopped, not only in Agriculture but Transportation and Health and Welfare, the people in Manitoba will ask what is happening.
February 25, 1985

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) comes from West-mount, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) come from Bay Street. It appears that they, along with civil servants from Ottawa, are the only ones who will have representation on the committees. The sad part is that this has been done secretly and behind closed doors. Apparently the recommendations are in now. When the Budget comes down we will find that various programs, in agriculture and other aspects of our economy, have been wiped out without there having been representation from the private sector in any part of our country, with the exception of those from Toronto, Montreal, and the civil servants in Ottawa, who make all these decisions behind closed doors.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Government House Leader)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REVIEW OF PROGRAMS. (B) AGENDA OF FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the Hon. Member asking the question not only has his facts wrong, but has drawn wrong conclusions from those facts that he had available in front of him.
The Ministerial Task Force on Program Review is examining all the programs of the federal government to achieve better service to the public, less red tape and greater efficiency. Programs in support of the agricultural sector are one of the priority areas for review, to ensure that they are truly contributing to the stability, growth and competitiveness of the agri-food sector.
In this Field of joint federal and provincial jurisdiction it is important to examine potential areas of duplication in federal and provincial programs. A study team comprised of private sector individuals and public servants has been formed to examine the results of federal programs. These people are consulting with groups benefiting from the programs. They are trying to determine whether there are any clear overlaps.
The study team has met with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). Members of the study team have met with the Deputy Minister of Agriculture and all senior officers of the Department to understand their view on the effectiveness and efficiency of their programs.
The team is also meeting with knowledgeable people in the private sector in both western and eastern Canada who can give first-hand knowledge and advice on areas of duplication or overlap, or where programs simply do not contribute to the strength of a dynamic agri-food sector which is so important to Canada's future economic prospects.
The study team indicates that it has received the fullest co-operation from all those contacted, from Ministers to officials to private individuals. Clearly all of them are enthusiastic about the future growth prospects of the agri-food sector, and want to see federal programs playing the most productive role possible to bring about that future.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL-REQUEST THAT PEACE CAMP BE REMOVED
PARLIAMENT HILL-REQUEST THAT PEACE CAMP BE REMOVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 13, five days after this House commenced, I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) a question with respect to the peace camp that he has located on Parliament Hill. The Minister replied:
I have the impression that my colleague is asking me to do in a few weeks something which the previous government failed to do in 18 months.
That was a few weeks then, Mr. Speaker; but that was November 13 and we have seen December 13, January 13, February 13, and soon it will be March 13. The Minister does nothing. This is a trespass on the lawns of Parliament Hill. Here we have the property of the people of Canada being used in a fashion that is not complimentary to this cherished place, the House of Parliament here in Ottawa.
Not only has this Minister refused to do something about that which is his responsibility to guard, the efficacy of this Parliament, but he refuses to come to grips with the problem. He says "Oh, they will move away when winter comes". That was on November 13. Winter has come and winter has just about gone and the peace camp still has not moved away. It has been here now for nearly two years. It will soon be past its second anniversary, yet the matter stays the way it is.
In a question I placed on the Order Paper I asked the Minister whether he intended to set up fees for those who would like to establish further protest camps on Parliament Hill. The Minister responded that the Government had no intention of setting out a new fee schedule. Presumably it is the intention of the Government to allow anybody-everybody and sundry-who wishes to protest to set up a camp on the lawns of Parliament.
Where is this Government going with respect to its responsibilities to guard Parliament? I say seriously that the Government has an obligation to bring forward a Bill, if necessary, in order to charge the users of the front lawns of Parliament Hill with trespass and move these trespassers from the front lawns of the Parliament Buildings. In spite of everything which has been done to bring the matter to the attention of the Government, nothing has happened.
I have been approached by not only citizens generally, but by people who work in the House who are concerned about the way the House is being denigrated by the existence of that camp on the front lawn. If something is not done very soon, other groups around the country will be setting up tents. Is it the intention of the Government to continue to allow this? If that is the intention, to continue to allow protests on Parliament Hill-something which does not exist in any other civilized country in the world-then let the Government say so, and let us have a debate in the House with respect to such camps. Surely somewhere along the line Parliament Hill has to be given some degree of respect. This camp is a disrespect of Parliament, and a disrespect of the democratic process.

February 25, 1985
Adjournment Debate
I do not know what reply the Ministry has given to the Parliamentary Secretary, but I certainly would not want to be in his position. There are all sorts of questions which could be asked with respect to the camp, but it must come down to this; if we are to continue to allow this type of thing to take place, Parliament will lose the respect the people should have for this institution. It is high time that the Government and the Minister faced their responsibilities in this regard.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board);
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL-REQUEST THAT PEACE CAMP BE REMOVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before getting into my formal reply, I should like to suggest that the Minister has in no way located the peace camp on Parliament Hill, as the Hon. Member unintentionally implied in his remarks.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) has replied to questions both oral and written on the subject of the peace camp, and the Minister does not intend to legislate the peace camp off the grounds of Parliament. This remains the policy of the present Government of Canada. Hon. Members on all sides of the House and the people of Canada support the notion of peace and those efforts made in the pursuit of an enduring peace throughout the world. This Government is committed to that goal.
What the Hon. Member raises is a question of a totally different nature. The Government and the citizens of the country must ask themselves whether the peace camp is setting a precedent which may be followed by other groups, and to what extend this should be allowed when in fact this action may impede access by all Canadians to the grounds and institutions of this Parliament which rightfully belong to them. There have been editorials and letters in newspapers across the
country which have either applauded or denounced the presence of the peace camp on Parliament Hill. What is most unfortunate is that the physical presence now becomes the issue rather than the quest for peace. We are focusing on this physical presence rather than the moral presence.
Our responsibility as a Government is to maintain Parliament Hill for all Canadians, as a space for all Canadians to enjoy-Canadians from every region and with different political viewpoints who wish to visit Parliament Hill. We as a Government wonder at what point the peace camp people will understand that they have made their points, and that by remaining there they will not change this Government's resolve to work hard for global harmony. What its physical presence does is spark a controversy over the physical presence rather than drawing attention to the point they want to make.
The Hon. Member has referred to the possibility of other groups setting up. We suggest that would be an unfortunate scenario, because that would really begin to hinder the ability of all Canadians and people from other countries to enjoy Parliament Hill. The grounds have long been of social pride for all Canadians and for people from other countries. They are a focal point of this nation's capital. We intend to see that they remain so.
In closing, I am informed that the Minister is continuing to study this issue and will make a statement in future weeks.
